item.title: What makes a laboratory self-driving? Mapping the SDL terminology landscape and introducing the FLEx categorization framework
item.description:
Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) are increasingly used to accelerate experimentation across chemistry, materials science, biotechnology, and related fields. Yet, the rapid development of autonomous experimentation has produced a fragmented terminology landscape in which overlapping terms, including autonomous laboratories, materials acceleration platforms, and robot scientists, are applied inconsistently. This complicates comparisons between systems and obscures what constitutes scientific autonomy. Here, we examine the definitions, historical development, disciplinary associations, and usage patterns of SDLs and related concepts. We further review existing approaches to categorizing autonomous laboratory systems and show that many rely on characteristics such as hardware complexity, system architecture, or human involvement that are difficult to apply consistently across disciplines and technologies. To provide a technology-independent alternative, we introduce the Feedback Loop Extent (FLEx) framework. FLEx classifies systems according to how far experimental feedback reaches into the scientific process, progressing from scripted execution without a scientific feedback loop to parameter optimization, autonomous experiment planning, hypothesis formulation, and scientific goal formulation. Applying FLEx to representative published systems shows that most contemporary SDLs autonomously plan experiments within human-defined objectives, whereas few demonstrably formulate hypotheses and none unambiguously reformulate broader scientific goals. FLEx provides a common language for distinguishing automation from different forms of autonomy and enables more transparent comparison and reporting of current and future SDLs.

Alexander Böser, Kjell Kochale, Patrick Courtney, Thorsten Teutenberg, Florian Boser, Guangqi Wu, Nikhil Deshpande, Christian P. Haas, Kaiman A. Cheung, Shuyuan Zhang, Radhika Gudipati, Alexei Lapkin, Frank Glorius, Stefan Bräse

item.title: Configuration-dependent hydrogen adsorption thermodynamics on S-doped RuO2(110): A first-principles study
item.description:
Rutile RuO2 has emerged as a promising non-platinum electrocatalyst for the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), yet its intrinsic activity is limited by strong hydrogen adsorption on coordinatively unsaturated Ru surface sites.Density functional theory calculations show that substitutional sulfur doping improves the HER adsorption thermodynamics of RuO2(110) by tuning hydrogen adsorption via local environment engineering. S doping weakens excessive hydrogen binding and drives the system toward near-optimal HER thermodynamics, approaching the benchmark ΔGH of Pt[3]. Symmetry-based enumeration and energetic screening were used to construct 86 inequivalent S-doped RuO2(110) models, from which four thermodynamically accessible configurations with favorable hydrogen adsorption were identified. The results reveal that dopant concentration governs the thermodynamic accessibility of S-doped configurations, whereas the local atomic configuration around the Ru active sites determines the hydrogen adsorption thermodynamics within the accessible concentration window. Among the accessible motifs, the 2S-top H adsorption site (H on the Ru adjacent to a single S dopant) is the most favorable, with ΔGH ≈ 0.06 eV, essentially equal to the 1S-top site (0.06 eV). Electronic structure analysis shows that S-induced hybridization between Ru 4d and dopant-derived p states leads to a downward shift of the Ru d-band center and reduced charge localization, tuning the hydrogen adsorption free energy from −0.26 eV on pristine RuO2 to approximately 0.06 eV.

Lihong Han, Ling Ding, Suwen Han, Yanan Zhang, Daquan Yang, Xiaoning Guan
